title: Angels (CCC 328–336)
hookLine: spiritual creatures, messengers, and a guardian beside each person

cards: Angels are everywhere. Chubby babies with harps on greeting cards. Women in white robes on top of Christmas trees.
People say someone who died has become an angel; a sweet kid gets called an angel. Almost none of that is what the Catholic Church actually teaches.
What it does teach is stranger, and in a way more comforting: that you have never, for one moment of your life, been completely alone. Today: angels.

teach.b: First, the word. Angel comes from the Greek angelos, messenger. Augustine made a sharp point, and the Catechism repeats it: angel is the name of their job, not their nature.
What they are is spirit; what they do is carry God's messages, like Gabriel at Nazareth, telling Mary she would bear a son. Second, what they are.
The Catechism, from paragraph 328, says the existence of angels is a truth of faith. They are purely spiritual creatures, with intelligence and will, personal and immortal. And they're created.

They are not God, and, despite the greeting cards, they're not people who died: when someone dies, Catholics pray they're with God, and the Church teaches they don't become angels. Third, the guardian.
Jesus says, in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "See that you despise not one of these little ones: for I say to you, that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven."
A psalm promises: "For he hath given his angels charge over thee; to keep thee in all thy ways."

The Catechism says that from infancy to death, human life is surrounded by the angels' watchful care, and quotes Saint Basil: beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd. Fourth, never alone.
Catholics keep the feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2, and there's a short traditional prayer to the guardian angel, often taught to children.

teach.h: TO KEEP THEE IN ALL THY WAYS.
teach.b: It's a small, steady comfort: on the dark nights, in the hospital hallway, on the drive home, Catholics believe someone God sent is keeping watch.

how: Catholics keep the feast of the Holy Guardian Angels on October 2 and of the archangels Michael, Gabriel and Raphael on September 29, and many families teach children the guardian angel prayer at bedtime.

o: a part of God sent out to visit the earth
a spirit God made to carry his messages
a good person who has died and gone to heaven

s: people become angels when they die
angels are a distinct kind of creature; Catholics pray the dead are with God, not that they become angels.
for Augustine, angel names a job, not a nature
their nature is spirit; their office is messenger.
Jesus speaks of the little ones' angels seeing God's face
Matthew 18:10, a key text for guardian angels.

games.q: a child asks: is grandpa an angel now? what does Catholic teaching say?
o: no; angels are a different kind of creature, and Catholics pray grandpa is with God
no one can know anything about it
games.why: the Catechism describes angels as purely spiritual creatures made by God. the dead don't become angels; Catholics pray for them and hope they're with God.

practice: The guardian angel prayer goes: Angel of God, my guardian dear, to whom God's love commits me here, ever this day be at my side, to light and guard, to rule and guide. Amen.
If you pray, say it once, slowly, on your own; if you don't, sit for a minute with the idea that someone might be keeping watch beside you, right now, and notice how that feels.

wordCard.voice: Angel. From the Greek for messenger: a spiritual creature made by God, and in Catholic belief, a guardian beside each person. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: messenger, the word behind angel.

carryVoice: Your line: never alone. In the lonely moments, the Church's promise is that someone is keeping watch. Three hundred days on the path.
